content: Chronic loss of appetite in individuals with cystic fibrosis is a significant concern for both patients and their families. Appetite stimulants have been utilized to help these patients achieve an optimal body mass index (BMI) and improve their nutritional status. However, the use of these medications may also lead to adverse effects on clinical outcomes. This review represents an updated evaluation of the evidence regarding the use of appetite stimulants in this population. The primary objective of this review was to systematically assess the evidence for the beneficial effects of appetite stimulants in managing anorexia associated with cystic fibrosis and to document any reported side effects. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted, including the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Trials Register, online trial registries, reference lists, and consultations with local and international experts. The last searches were conducted in May 2022. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared appetite stimulants to placebo, no treatment, or other appetite stimulants, or that compared different doses or regimens of the same stimulant. Eligible studies involved adults and children with cystic fibrosis and had a minimum duration of one month. Four trials, involving a total of 70 participants, were included in the review. These trials compared the appetite stimulants cyproheptadine hydrochloride and megestrol acetate to placebo. However, the number of adults and children in each trial was not consistently reported. The certainty of the evidence was assessed as low due to the small sample sizes, incomplete or selective outcome reporting, and unclear risks of selection bias. For the primary outcomes, a meta-analysis of two trials (42 participants) suggested that appetite stimulants may lead to a greater increase in weight (mean difference [MD] 1.25 kg, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.45 to 2.05) at three months. One trial (17 participants) showed a similar result at six months (MD 3.80 kg, 95% CI 1.27 to 6.33). The weight z score also appeared to improve with appetite stimulants compared to placebo at three months (MD 0.61, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.93; 3 studies; 40 participants) and at six months (MD 0.74, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.22; 1 trial; 17 participants). There was no evidence to suggest a difference in efficacy between cyproheptadine hydrochloride and megestrol acetate for these outcomes. Regarding body composition, only one trial (25 participants) provided analyzable data for BMI, with results favoring cyproheptadine hydrochloride over placebo. Another trial (16 participants) supported this finding narratively. Lung function, measured as forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) % predicted, was reported in all four trials over durations ranging from two to nine months. Two trials (42 participants) found that appetite stimulants may have little or no effect on FEV1 % predicted at three months, and one trial (17 participants) reported similar findings at six months. Two additional trials provided narrative support for these results. Limited data were available for secondary outcomes. Two trials (23 participants) suggested that appetite stimulants may increase appetite compared to placebo at three months (odds ratio 45.25, 95% CI 3.57 to 573.33). Only one study assessed quality of life, reporting that cyproheptadine reduced fatigue in two participants compared to none in the placebo group. Another study (25 participants) found no difference in energy intake between appetite stimulants and placebo at three months. Adverse effects were insufficiently reported, preventing a comprehensive assessment of their impact. Two studies (33 participants) narratively reported similar antibiotic requirements between appetite stimulants and placebo at three months. In conclusion, at six months, appetite stimulants appeared to improve weight (or weight z score) and self-reported appetite in adults and children with cystic fibrosis. However, the evidence supporting these findings is of low certainty due to the small number of trials and participants. The impact of side effects remains unclear due to insufficient reporting. While the data suggest a potential role for appetite stimulants in managing anorexia in this population, firm conclusions cannot be drawn. Clinicians prescribing these medications should remain vigilant for potential adverse effects and monitor patients closely. Further research is needed to identify meaningful surrogate measures for appetite and to define what constitutes quality weight gain. Future trials should employ validated tools, including disease-specific instruments for assessing poor appetite. This review underscores the need for multicenter, adequately powered, and well-designed trials to evaluate the safety and efficacy of appetite stimulants in individuals with cystic fibrosis and to establish the optimal treatment approach.
